text: Creating a storage account or S3 bucket is one command — the real deployment decision is what happens right after: deciding exactly who, and what, is allowed to reach it. Skip that step and you've deployed working storage with the wrong security posture, which is an easier mistake to make than it sounds, because the storage itself works fine either way.

az storage account create with --allow-blob-public-access false turns off anonymous public read access at the account level, and --default-action Deny means the account's firewall denies every request by default — including from inside Azure — until a rule explicitly allows it. The network-rule add call that follows then opens exactly one path in: traffic from snet-app-tier, the specific subnet Lesson 9's VM is sitting in. Nothing else gets through unless a later rule deliberately adds it.

create-bucket alone doesn't make a bucket public — new buckets already default to private — but it also doesn't guarantee the bucket stays that way if someone later attaches a permissive bucket policy or ACL. put-public-access-block, with all four settings set to true, is the explicit, account-level guarantee: no ACL, no bucket policy, and no cross-account grant can make this bucket or its objects public, no matter what gets configured on it later.

Neither of these commands grants anyone actual read or write access yet — they just lock the door. The next lesson, wiring compute to storage, is where the one VM or EC2 instance that genuinely needs to reach this storage gets a specific, scoped grant: a role assignment in Azure, an IAM policy in AWS. That order — lock it down, then open exactly one path — is deliberate, the same order this program has used for secrets and IAM since the identity chapters.

A storage account or bucket that was created successfully but never locked down this way is still the wrong outcome, even though nothing about it looks broken. Next up: wiring the one VM or EC2 instance that needs this storage to it correctly — a managed identity or IAM role granted a scoped permission, not a credential embedded anywhere in code.
